talks.title: Searching The Invisible Internet
talks.teaser: Deep web research and reconnaissance on hidden internet resources.
talks.summary:
### The Attacker's Perspective: Mapping Shadow IT
At 00:00, renowned web security pioneer Robert Hansen (widely known in the hacker community as RSnake) takes the stage at r00tz Asylum to teach young hackers how adversaries map corporate targets. Reflecting on over twenty years in cybersecurity, Hansen explains that before an attacker ever launches an exploit, they conduct exhaustive reconnaissance to discover the "invisible internet"—the forgotten servers, unlinked testing portals, orphaned subdomains, and shadow IT assets that organizations deploy but fail to inventory or protect.

### Corporate Conglomerates and Acquisition Blind Spots
At 01:31 and 03:02, Hansen examines how corporate growth creates massive security blind spots. Major enterprise conglomerates (such as Sears acquiring Kmart) routinely inherit thousands of disparate legacy networks, regional distribution systems, and abandoned web properties. Because different business units deploy servers independently without centralized IT coordination, large companies frequently lose track of their own digital footprints, leaving exposed assets completely unmonitored.

### Uncovering Hidden Infrastructure via OSINT and Proxies
At 04:33, Hansen illustrates the primary methodologies used to expose hidden infrastructure using Open Source Intelligence (OSINT). While companies often place modern proxy servers and web application firewalls in front of their primary domains, attackers bypass these protections by searching for origin IP addresses, scanning adjacent CIDR blocks, and querying passive DNS records. By uncovering unproxied direct connections to backend infrastructure, an adversary can attack the origin servers directly.

### The Inherent Vulnerability of Staging and Orphaned Endpoints
At 06:04, the presentation examines why shadow infrastructure presents the most lucrative target for attackers. While production web portals receive regular vulnerability audits and security patching, development environments and staging servers often run obsolete software stacks with default administrative credentials. Hansen emphasizes that organizations frequently invest millions in hardening their primary domain while leaving wide-open, unpatched backdoors on obscure testing subdomains.

### Foundational Asset Hygiene for Future Defenders
Concluding between 06:50 and 07:34, Hansen delivers a fundamental lesson in cybersecurity: you cannot defend what you do not know you own. He advises aspiring defenders to continuously perform attack-surface mapping against their own networks, proactively retiring abandoned infrastructure and maintaining comprehensive asset inventories. By adopting an attacker's reconnaissance mindset, young security professionals can eliminate perimeter blind spots before adversaries find them.

talks.title: Tips for Internet Privacy at College
talks.teaser: Privacy protection strategies for college students online.
talks.summary:
### Privacy Risks on Campus and Dormitory Networks
At 00:00, Patrick McCanna presents practical cybersecurity and privacy advice for students entering college at r00tz Asylum. McCanna explains that campus Wi-Fi networks and shared dorm connections operate as untrusted, hostile local networks where thousands of student devices reside on shared subnets without enterprise segmentation.

### Patching, Wi-Fi Hygiene, and Disabling Auto-Connect
At 02:26, McCanna emphasizes the necessity of installing operating system updates promptly, citing recent hardware-level Wi-Fi vulnerabilities such as Broadpwn. He advises students to disable automatic connection to open Wi-Fi hotspots, turn off Bluetooth when not in active use, and avoid connecting laptops directly to unencrypted campus networks without protection.

### Disabling Insecure Local File Sharing
At 04:50, the talk highlights common configuration oversights when students transition from home networks to dormitories. Services such as Windows file sharing, SMB, and unrestricted AirDrop frequently remain enabled by default, exposing private academic files and personal media to anyone on the same campus network subnet.

### Guarding Against Orientation Social Engineering
At 07:13, McCanna warns against oversharing during freshman orientation icebreakers and social mixers. Casual social questions regarding hometowns, high schools, childhood pets, and family members directly mirror common security challenge questions used for account recovery, enabling acquaintances to perform targeted credential resets.

### Password Managers and Multi-Factor Authentication
Concluding between 09:50 and 15:21, McCanna reviews foundational operational security habits. He urges students to adopt dedicated password managers, check for compromised accounts on Have I Been Pwned, separate academic from personal email accounts, and replace insecure SMS verification with app-based multi-factor authentication.

talks.title: Everything You Need To Know About The US Dept of Justice
talks.teaser: Legal context and implications for hackers regarding US Department of Justice.
talks.summary:
### The Role of the Department of Justice in Cybersecurity
At 00:00, Leonard Bailey, Special Counsel for National Security in the Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section (CCIPS) at the US Department of Justice (DOJ), introduces the federal government's perspective on computer crime. Bailey outlines the mission of CCIPS, explaining how federal prosecutors and cyber investigators work to counter transnational cybercrime, dismantle botnets, and prosecute criminal malicious hackers.

### Collaboration Between Federal Law Enforcement and Hackers
At 03:40 and 07:30, Bailey emphasizes the critical partnership between federal authorities and the legitimate white-hat security community. He highlights coordinated botnet takedowns—such as the legal and technical actions executed to sinkhole the Gameover Zeus banking trojan and mitigate the Mirai IoT botnet after its devastating October 2016 attack on Dyn DNS. He explains how private threat researchers provide the essential reverse engineering and intelligence that enables federal courts to issue emergency seizure warrants.

### Navigating the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA)
At 09:15, the speaker addresses the primary federal cyber statute: the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA). Bailey demystifies common misconceptions regarding federal prosecution, clarifying the legal boundary between authorized security research and illegal unauthorized access. He explains the Department's policy guidance governing CFAA prosecutions, emphasizing that the DOJ focuses enforcement efforts on malicious bad actors and financial theft rather than ethical security researchers practicing responsible disclosure.

### Safe Harbor, Bug Bounties, and Legal Precedents
At 11:45, the presentation discusses the rapid emergence of corporate bug bounty programs and governmental vulnerability disclosure initiatives (such as "Hack the Pentagon"). Bailey explains how formalized safe harbor policies provide legal authorization for security researchers to audit systems without fear of prosecution, bridging historical friction between the federal legal system and the hacker underground.

### Pursuing Public-Interest Careers in Cyber Law and Defense
Concluding between 12:50 and 13:33, Bailey encourages the young attendees at r00tz Asylum to consider public-service careers in digital forensics, technology policy, and cyber law. He stresses that protecting the nation's critical infrastructure requires technically sophisticated professionals who combine deep computer science expertise with a commitment to civil liberties and ethical public defense.

talks.title: Hacking & Robotics v2 point 0
talks.teaser: Robotics security and hacking techniques for automated systems.
talks.summary:
### Introducing the Hacker Mindset Through Robotics
At 00:00, STEM educator Erin Owens opens her presentation at r00tz Asylum, titled "Hacking & Robotics v2.0." Owens introduces young hackers to the creative convergence of robotics, embedded microcontrollers, and computer programming. She emphasizes that building and programming autonomous robots is one of the most effective, hands-on gateways for understanding the core tenets of computer hardware and software engineering.

### The FIRST LEGO League Core Values
At 03:20, Owens reviews the cultural philosophy of the FIRST LEGO League (FLL) robotics program, highlighting its foundational Core Values: "Gracious Professionalism" and "Coopertition." She challenges students to recognize that the technical superpowers gained through programming and robotics must be applied constructively for social good. True hacker culture, Owens explains, is built on collaboration, mutual respect, and sharing solutions with competitors rather than destructive exploitation.

### Programming Autonomous Robots and Sensor Feedback
At 07:36, the presentation examines the technical workstation environment for developing robotic autonomy using LEGO Mindstorms, Arduino, and micro-Python platforms. Owens breaks down sensor integration, demonstrating how light sensors, ultrasonic distance sensors, and gyroscopes feed continuous data streams into control loops. She explains how algorithms process sensor feedback to navigate physical obstacles and execute precision tasks without human intervention.

### Red Team vs. Blue Team Concepts in Cyber-Physical Systems
At 10:15, Owens translates enterprise cybersecurity roles into robotics education. She explains how robotic development mirrors red team (offensive penetration testing) and blue team (defensive engineering) dynamics. While offensive thinkers identify how external conditions or malicious inputs can disrupt an autonomous robot, defenders engineer error-handling routines, physical shielding, and fail-safe mechanisms to ensure continuous operation.

### Safe Experimentation and Building Future Tech
Concluding between 12:30 and 13:40, Owens coordinates safe flight and robotics demonstrations with the audience. She encourages young participants to dismantle broken consumer electronics, experiment with open-source microcontrollers, and embrace iterative trial-and-error in their home workshops, emphasizing that learning from system failures is the cornerstone of engineering excellence.

talks.title: Home Depot and A Plan of Attack for Hackers
talks.teaser: Physical reconnaissance and social engineering techniques for hacking public spaces.
talks.summary:
### Finding Hacker Projects in Everyday Hardware Stores
At 00:00, renowned physical security expert and lockpicker Deviant Ollam takes the stage at r00tz Asylum to challenge traditional definitions of hacking. Ollam explains that while most people associate hacking with computer keyboards and computer screens, the true hacker mindset is about curiosity, physical problem-solving, and examining everyday objects to understand how they function. He frames the neighborhood Home Depot as a playground of raw components for curious makers.

### Lock Bypasses and Improvised Physical Security Tools
At 03:15 and 06:13, Ollam demonstrates how common materials found in the plumbing, electrical, and hardware aisles can be repurposed into bypass tools for physical security mechanisms. Using simple wire hangers, feeler gauges, plastic tubing, and universal drain stoppers, he shows how physical penetration testers construct under-door tools, latch-slipping shims, and emergency exit release triggers. He explains that mechanical security often relies on superficial barriers that fail against creative lateral thinking.

### Fabrication, Prototyping, and Fixing Broken Systems
At 08:45, the speaker inspires young attendees to reject modern throwaway consumer culture. When household appliances, electronics, or tools break, Ollam urges youth to disassemble them, diagnose the point of failure, and attempt repairs before discarding them. He walks through basic physical fabrication skills—including using heat shrink tubing, hand tools, fasteners, and adhesives—to construct durable custom cases, portable antenna mounts, and electronics enclosures.

### The Engineering Principles of Physical Resilience
At 10:30 and 12:16, Ollam explains the structural engineering principles behind physical security hardware. He discusses material science, examining how metals resist shear stress, how padlocks withstand cutting and prying attacks, and how environmental factors like corrosion impact security integrity. He emphasizes that understanding physical durability enables hackers to evaluate both mechanical and digital systems with a critical engineering eye.

### Nurturing Curiosity and Hands-On Self-Sufficiency
Concluding his talk, Ollam delivers an empowering message on technical self-reliance. He encourages kids and teenagers to look at the physical world with the same inquisitiveness they apply to video games and computers. By developing practical fabrication skills and embracing the challenge of hands-on physical problem-solving, young hackers build the confidence and ingenuity necessary to excel in any technical field.

talks.title: Introduction To Cheat Engine
talks.teaser: Cheat Engine tools and techniques for game modification and binary analysis.
talks.summary:
### Introduction to Game Hacking with Cheat Engine
At 00:00, speaker David delivers an introductory workshop at r00tz Asylum exploring the fundamentals of reverse engineering and memory modification using Cheat Engine. The session is designed to teach younger hackers how software programs execute in memory and how process values can be analyzed and manipulated in real time.

### Process Memory Scanning and Value Filtering
At 02:07 and 04:14, David explains how operating systems allocate memory addresses to running applications. Using Cheat Engine attached to a Game Boy Advance emulator running Pokémon, he demonstrates searching for specific numeric variables, altering the in-game state, and re-scanning memory to isolate the exact address controlling player experience levels and Pokémon statistics.

### Modifying Inventory States and Byte Editing
At 07:03 and 10:02, the demonstration transitions to Minecraft to illustrate dynamic inventory editing. David shows how to identify memory addresses corresponding to item stacks by repeatedly searching, discarding a single unit, and filtering for decreased values. Once isolated, the memory value is frozen and edited, turning an ordinary three-block stack into hundreds of diamond items.

### Tracking and Manipulating Spatial Coordinates
At 12:03 and 16:11, David delves into advanced memory manipulation by locating the player's 3D XYZ spatial coordinates. Pairing Cheat Engine with an NBT editor, he demonstrates finding floating-point position coordinates within process RAM and altering them to teleport the player across the map, illustrating how game engines process positional vectors and player movement data.

talks.title: You are not a Digital Native and that's OK
talks.teaser: Digital literacy and technology education for the next generation.
talks.summary:
### Deconstructing the "Digital Native" Fallacy
At 00:00, acclaimed science-fiction author, activist, and journalist Cory Doctorow takes the stage at r00tz Asylum to deliver a thought-provoking keynote. Doctorow begins by dismantling the widespread cultural myth of the "digital native"—the assumption that because young people were born into a world saturated with smartphones and touchscreens, they automatically possess an innate understanding of technology. Doctorow argues that being surrounded by commercial gadgets does not make one technologically literate any more than living near a highway makes one an automotive mechanic.

### Walled Gardens vs. General-Purpose Computing
At 05:20 and 10:36, Doctorow contrasts the open computing architecture of early personal computers with the locked-down "walled gardens" of modern mobile ecosystems. Proprietary app stores, locked bootloaders, and corporate digital rights management (DRM) are deliberately engineered to prevent users from inspecting, modifying, or repairing their own devices. Doctorow warns that when technology corporations control what software can be executed, users are reduced from autonomous technology owners to passive digital consumers.

### Packet Inspection and the Architecture of the Internet
At 13:15, Doctorow explains the vital importance of learning how the internet actually works. He emphasizes that the fundamental protocol design of the internet—an open, decentralized network of general-purpose computers passing packetized data—is inherently democratic. He encourages youth to look beneath slick graphical interfaces by learning to program, inspecting network packets, and understanding how data routes across global infrastructure.

### The Politics of Technology and Digital Rights
At 16:40, the presentation explores the political and legal dimensions of computer security. Doctorow references the r00tz Code of Ethics, explaining that technical knowledge carries immense civic responsibility. He discusses how corporate monopolies and governmental surveillance apparatuses leverage opaque technology to monitor citizens, suppress competition, and curtail free speech, emphasizing that understanding computing is essential for defending civil liberties.

### Reclaiming Technological Agency and Empowerment
Concluding between 18:20 and 19:41, Doctorow delivers an inspiring call to action for the next generation. He tells the young audience that it is completely acceptable not to know everything today, but urges them to never accept the passive role assigned to them by technology conglomerates. By learning to code, reverse-engineer hardware, and question technical authority, young hackers can build open systems that preserve human freedom.

talks.title: Arm Mounted Weaponized Platform and Anime Viewer
talks.teaser: Wearable hardware projects combining security tools with entertainment devices.
talks.summary:
### Concept and Hardware Architecture of the Forearm Cyberdeck
At 00:00, Corbin Vila introduces his custom-built, arm-mounted wearable hacking terminal and media player presented at r00tz Asylum. Vila describes the mechanical and electronic construction of the forearm rig, powered by a Raspberry Pi running Linux, a compact LCD display, rechargeable battery pack, and custom hardware input buttons.

### Non-Discoverable Bluetooth Sniffing with Ubertooth One
At 01:18 and 04:35, Vila details the integration of an Ubertooth One software-defined radio module. He explains how standard Bluetooth adapters only identify devices in discoverable mode, whereas the Ubertooth sniffs raw 2.4 GHz packets over the air to uncover discoverable and non-discoverable devices alike, identifying nearby laptops, phones, and peripherals by MAC address and manufacturer.

### GPIO Interfacing and Automated Sniffing Scripts
At 02:41 and 05:48, the speaker walks through the Python software controlling the wearable. Custom scripts poll the Raspberry Pi's GPIO pins to handle tactile button inputs, enabling the user to quickly cycle between active Wi-Fi packet capturing, Bluetooth reconnaissance dashboards, and local video playback for watching anime.

talks.title: Hacking an Insecure WiFi Camera
talks.teaser: Wireless security vulnerabilities in consumer IoT cameras and exploitation techniques.
talks.summary:
### The Pervasive Insecurities of Budget Consumer IoT
At 00:00, Aron Rosenberg and Aaron Standridge open their presentation at r00tz Asylum by examining the security shortcomings of cheap, internet-connected consumer security cameras. As smart home adoption surges, millions of consumers purchase low-cost Wi-Fi webcams to monitor their homes and families, operating under the dangerous assumption that commercial products implement baseline cybersecurity protections.

### Network Reconnaissance and Port Scanning
At 02:40 and 04:15, the speakers demonstrate initial network reconnaissance against a newly purchased Wi-Fi camera on an isolated test network. Using basic port scanning tools, they reveal that the camera exposes multiple unauthenticated network services, including an open Telnet management port (port 23), an insecure HTTP administrative web interface, and an unencrypted Real-Time Streaming Protocol (RTSP) video stream on port 554.

### Trivial Administrative Bypass and Default Credentials
At 06:03, Rosenberg and Standridge showcase how easily these devices are compromised. They demonstrate that the camera's administrative web interface and Telnet daemon ship with ubiquitous default credentials (`admin`/`admin` or blank passwords) that the setup software never prompts the owner to change. An attacker on the local network—or on the wider internet if universal plug-and-play (UPnP) is active—can gain complete root administrative control over the camera in seconds.

### Sniffing Live RTSP Streams and Video Feeds
At 08:20, the presenters illustrate the privacy invasion resulting from unencrypted video streaming. By connecting a media player directly to the camera's RTSP endpoint without authentication, they display a live video and audio feed across the auditorium screen. They explain how an attacker on the same Wi-Fi network can effortlessly eavesdrop on private household rooms, listen to conversations, and record footage without the homeowner's knowledge.

### Secure Architecture: Client-Server Models and TLS Encryption
Concluding between 09:30 and 10:35, the authors contrast insecure peer-to-peer (P2P) cameras with properly engineered security architectures. They explain that secure IoT devices must mandate strong, unique setup passwords, disable unauthenticated legacy services like Telnet, and route all telemetry and video streaming through fully encrypted TLS tunnels utilizing a secure client-server model.
